Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Gameplay 2.1 Step 1: Play a Token 2.1.1 Check for First Territory 2.2 Step 2: Move the Guardian 3 Scoring Overview This is a safari themed popularity race. Be the person with the most tokens in the coloured territory and you'll score all the points for that territory. Be the first to complete a territory and you win the inauguration bonus worth 5 points. The player with the most points at the end of the game wins. Gameplay To complete setup, the first player will choose where the Guardian starts. Play then continues with the next player. On your turn you will do 2 actions, in order: Step 1: Play a Token You must place a token of your choice in the row/column the guardian is in. You put your token face up, then immediately take the following actions if the condition applies: When you place: Next to: Do this: Zebra Lion Flip the Zebra face down Lion Zebra(s) Flip all adjacent Zebras face down Gazelle Lion Flip the Gazelle face down Lion Gazelle(s) Return all adjacent Gazelles to owner Crocodile Gazelle (with a river in between) (optional) Crocodile and Gazelle swap places. If more than one Gazelle qualifies, choose one. Reaction can be chained based on the Crocodile's new location. If Gazelle is moved next to a lion, it is flipped face down. Crocodile Gazelle (no river in between) Does NOT trigger swap. Check for First Territory Do not check until you have completed all triggered actions. If any territory is full, take the Inauguration token (worth 5 points). Once taken, you will no longer check for this condition after Step 1. Step 2: Move the Guardian The Guardian moves clockwise. Move the Guardian 1-3 spaces forward, stopping in a row/column with at least 1 empty space. If there is not a legal option available, move the Guardian forward to the first available row/column with at least 1 empty space. Play continues with the next player. If they do not have any tokens remaining, play your remaining tokens, 1 at a time, until the board is full. Scoring For each territory, the player with the most tokens (face up or down) is the one to score the territory. Count up all visible points in the territory. The player with the Inauguration token scores 5 points. The player with the most points wins.

[Rating: 3/10] This is a two player area control that to me felt pretty boring.  I didn't really like the artwork and the variable powers of the tiles didn't even really excite me.  There is a low amount of luck, so I could see it being a decent title for some people and normally low luck is good for me, but it almost felt more like an abstract strategy game than an area majority which probably what turned me off of this game.

[Rating: 4/10] Nice little game.  It plays quickly, makes sense thematically and is kind of fun!  I wouldn't want to play with someone who would analyze it to death.  This in a way seems similar to Kupferkessel Company in the way that the movement of "Impala Jones" around the edge of the board limits your choices.

[Rating: 4/10] Simple concept, but really easy to lose miserably with no chance for a comeback. Probably won't play it again.

[Rating: 5/10] Really, this is just an abstract game with a thin theme. However, it's a fun little game and very quick. I believe this would be a very good game to teach older kids and teens, to help them develop strategies without overwhelming them with gameplay.

[Rating: 5/10] It's a cute little game, but it wears out quite quickly. The mechanics are truly innovative, and work well within the game. However, the game, while elegant, is not that fun.  The rating might go up with further plays, though.

[Rating: 5/10] The idea is original but it's not that fun as it seems to be. You can almost calculate everything but the more you calculate the less there is fun...

[Rating: 5/10] This is an interesting area control game on a grid. I wouldn't run to play it again, but it had some interesting concepts.

[Rating: 5/10] 07.2026  I was drawn to Zèbres because it’s a grid-based game that reminds me a bit of the territory claiming in Nuggets with the shared-pawn movement of Butterfly. While the premise sounds great on paper, it felt somewhat lackluster after a couple of plays where players settle into a pattern of placing non-committal gazelles initially, then trying to boost scores by playing zebras later on; and then placing some of the more impactful pieces—the crocs, elephant, and lion in the mid to late game.
